games.explanation: Yesavage's overall line reads like an ace, but split the numbers by handedness and the illusion falls apart in a hurry. Right-handed bats have shredded him at a .332 xwOBA clip, and Boston happens to be running Contreras, Abreu, and Rafaela straight at him, exactly the kind of hard-contact righty group his profile can't survive. The walks are the tell here, nearly 13% against same-side hitters, which is what happens when a young arm nibbles because he doesn't trust the zone. Fenway plays up for runs, the wind is a non-factor, and the better team is being priced like a coinflip. -124 on the side with the pitching mismatch and the lineup edge is the whole story.

Jacob Lopez walks the yard and gives up loud contact to righties, which is a problem when the other dugout has Buxton and Bell waiting for exactly that arm. The splits tell on him: against right-handed bats his xwOBA jumps almost fifty points, and the barrel rate he surrenders nearly quadruples. Minnesota is also the meaningfully better team here, with an Elo gap that says this line should be closer to -160 than -140. Yes, Zebby Matthews is the softer half of the pitching matchup, but a hitter's park with the wind blowing out favors the lineup that actually squares balls up. Pay the -140 and let the better roster do the work.

Dustin May is being priced like a stopper when he's really a walk machine who lets everyone hit the ball hard, and Cincinnati happens to be the kind of lineup that punishes exactly that. May is handing out free passes at better than a double-digit clip while getting barreled at a rate that should embarrass a big-league starter, and the Reds have the right-handed thump (Elly, Stewart, Steer) to turn those mistakes into damage. The park plays neutral, the wind is nudging balls back into the yard, and the sim still spits out Cincinnati as the better side in a tight one. Getting +140 on a coin flip your opponent doesn't realize is a coin flip is how the bankroll grows.

Logan Webb is a very good pitcher priced like an unbeatable one, and the Angels are exactly the kind of righty-heavy lineup that treats him like a mortal. Webb's numbers against right-handed bats are strong on the surface, but Neto and Trout are the profile that gives ground-ball command guys trouble, and Oracle Park doesn't rescue a starter from a lineup that hits the ball hard rather than lifting it. The Giants counter with an offense fronted by a slap hitter and not much thump behind him, which is how you end up with a projected one-run game the board has quietly turned into a mismatch. Getting a coin flip at +146 is the entire argument.
